overview: Aymara-speaking communities built several powerful highland societies around Lake Titicaca and beyond. They were never one timeless kingdom. The linked map records span 1279 to 1500; their outlines simplify overlapping peoples and territories, especially the southern extension toward the Atacama. Aymara history continues today.

periods.title: Highland polities
periods.summary: Aymara-speaking communities consolidated varied highland political formations during these centuries.

periods.title: Inca expansion
periods.summary: Military struggles and negotiated arrangements brought Aymara polities into the Inca state, often with substantial local autonomy.

periods.title: Colonial transformation
periods.summary: Spanish settlement and labor policies disrupted older connections between highland and valley communities.

periods.title: Continuing communities
periods.summary: Aymara language and cultural knowledge remain living concerns across Bolivia, Chile and Peru.

items.text: Ayllus connected households into larger social groups. Some Aymara polities organized upper and lower divisions, with several levels of leadership. Calling them kingdoms is convenient, but it can hide authority shared among different leaders and communities.

Families and leaders maintained links to farming settlements at different elevations. Highland herders could obtain valley crops through relatives and exchanges across these scattered territories. Political geography could resemble an archipelago on land, with long journeys between its islands.

At Sillustani beside Lake Umayo, the official inventory records 91 funerary towers from different periods. Some use carefully fitted stone and others rough masonry. The site preserves a changing tradition of commemorating the dead across Colla and Inca rule.

Sillustani’s best-known tower is named for a lizard carved on a stone block. It rises about 12 meters, with a base over seven meters across. A small carved animal and an enormous structure can belong to the same architectural project.

Across the cold Andean highlands, farmers make chuño by letting potatoes freeze at night and dry during sunny days. Trampling removes moisture and skins. Properly dried potatoes can keep for years: winter weather becomes part of the pantry’s equipment.

A museum’s evidence for that food need not be ancient. Michigan’s collection includes chuño bought in a Cusco grocery in 1966. Such specimens help document a living food technology alongside the much older accounts of Andean potato preservation.

An Aymara tunic from Bolivia in the Metropolitan Museum dates to the late eighteenth century. It is woven from camelid hair and measures roughly 67 by 89 centimeters. A surviving garment makes the skilled handling of animal fibers tangible.

A twentieth-century Aymara tupu in Chile’s pre-Columbian museum combines silver and glass. This large pin fastened or adorned women’s clothing at the chest. Everyday dress can carry metalworking skill and an enduring emblem of identity.

María Choque told an interviewer in 2023 that she began making thread at six, taught by her grandmother. Socks and hats came before more demanding garments. Her account gives one family’s learning sequence, from watching an elder to mastering difficult work.

The same reporting describes October shearing that leaves wool on the animals for warmth. During February festivities, families attach wool flowers and pompoms to camelids. Even the suppliers of the wool can end up wearing some of the decoration.

A modern Chilean schoolbook prints “Kamisaraki jilata”, meaning “How are you, brother?” It appears in Estela Gamero’s bilingual greeting song. These Latin letters record living Aymara; the sample is from a present-day teaching resource, not an ancient inscription.

Spanish authorities forced Karanqas communities into concentrated towns and demanded labor for the Potosí mines. These policies separated people from land and strained households. Colonial rule transformed local institutions, but Aymara communities kept rebuilding relationships and practices across the region.

ending.text: Inca conquest and Spanish colonization changed Aymara political autonomy and landholding. Neither ended the people or their language. The map’s 1492 and 1500 endpoints are display boundaries; modern communities in Bolivia, Chile and Peru continue teaching, weaving, farming and organizing their cultural life.
